report:
**Conclusion:** Your blanket “false” judgment is not supported. The best available evidence suggests that *improving bedroom ventilation* can modestly improve sleep, and opening a window is one way to do that. But it is not a universal sleep remedy, and evidence remains limited.

A 2015 controlled field study in student dorm rooms compared ventilation conditions for a week each. Sleep was measured with actigraphy plus morning reports; bedroom temperature did not differ between conditions, helping isolate air quality/ventilation. It found better sleep-related outcomes and next-day performance with better ventilation.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26452168/

More directly, a 2022 two-week field intervention in 40 Danish bedrooms found that opening a window, door, or both reduced overnight CO₂. Sleep quality and next-day cognitive performance improved when the intervention reduced CO₂ by at least 200 ppm; however, the search report indicates objective and subjective sleep improvements occurred **only when the window was open**, not reliably with door-opening alone.  
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132322008605

This is biologically plausible—an open door/window can dilute occupants’ CO₂ and other indoor pollutants—but the claim should be phrased as “may improve sleep *when it meaningfully improves ventilation*,” rather than as a guarantee. The literature review itself stresses that evidence on bedroom ventilation’s sleep consequences has been relatively sparse.  
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132320306004

Practical caveat: do not trade stale air for disruptive outdoor noise, allergens, smoke, unsafe temperatures, or pollution. Mechanical ventilation or a suitably filtered system may be preferable where those conditions apply.
